articles.title: Ciclone traz temporais ao Sul; frente fria derruba temperaturas | G1
articles.standfirst: Santa Catarina pode ter chuva acima de 100 mm nesta segunda (31), além de granizo e vento forte. Em São Paulo, a chuva aumenta entre esta tarde e terça-feira (1º), depois de dias de calor.
articles.summary: Santa Catarina pode ter chuva acima de 100 mm, além de granizo e vento forte. No Sudeste, a frente fria aumenta a chuva e faz as temperaturas caírem nos próximos dias.
articles.body:
Imagem de satélite mostra a presença de nuvens sobre a América do Sul nesta segunda-feira (31). — Foto: CPTEC/Inpe

A última tarde de agosto será marcada por temporais no Sul e aumento da chuva no Sudeste, com a formação de um novo ciclone extratropical e o avanço de uma frente fria pelo país.

🌀 ENTENDA: Os ciclones extratropicais são sistemas de baixa pressão atmosférica – regiões causadoras de tempo adverso em grande escala – que surgem normalmente em latitudes médias. Eles são formados pelo contraste de temperaturas de diferentes massas de ar (quente e fria).

Segundo a Climatempo, uma área de baixa pressão atravessa o Sul nesta segunda-feira (31), ajuda a formar o ciclone no oceano e vai dar origem à frente fria.

O maior risco de tempo severo nesta tarde fica entre Santa Catarina, o norte do Rio Grande do Sul e o Paraná, onde há possibilidade de chuva volumosa, granizo e rajadas fortes de vento.

⚠️ A formação de tornados também não está descartada em pontos de Santa Catarina e do Paraná.

A chuva pode passar dos 100 mm em áreas de Santa Catarina. O Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) também aponta os maiores volumes da semana para o Sul, principalmente em Santa Catarina e em áreas do norte gaúcho e do oeste do Paraná.

"Esse ciclone extratropical é que vai dar origem à frente fria que vai avançar em direção a São Paulo e provocar a grande mudança no tempo do começo do mês", afirma César Soares, meteorologista da Climatempo.

Na terça-feira (1º), a frente fria avança e espalha a chuva por outras áreas do Sudeste.

A previsão indica volumes mais elevados em partes de São Paulo e, na quarta-feira (2), a chuva alcança com mais força o Rio de Janeiro, o sul de Minas Gerais e o sul do Espírito Santo.

Antes da queda nas temperaturas, o calor ainda será forte em parte do Centro-Oeste, do Norte e do interior do Nordeste.

Segundo a Climatempo, áreas de Mato Grosso, Goiás, Tocantins e Piauí ainda podem se aproximar dos 40°C nesta segunda.

Cuiabá (MT) chegou a 41,2°C no domingo (30), novo recorde da capital em 2026.

Com a passagem da frente fria, as temperaturas diminuem nos próximos dias no Sul e em parte do Sudeste.

Nas áreas mais altas de Santa Catarina, as mínimas podem chegar perto dos 5°C na quarta-feira (2).

Temperaturas mínimas previstas para esta terça em todo o Brasil. — Foto: CPTEC/Inpe

No Sul, a queda será mais perceptível depois da passagem da chuva.

Na terça-feira (1º), as máximas já ficam mais baixas em boa parte da região e, na quarta, o frio ganha força principalmente nas áreas serranas de Santa Catarina e do Rio Grande do Sul.

No Sudeste, as temperaturas também recuam em pontos de maior altitude.

Em Minas Gerais, a previsão indica mínimas em torno de 10°C na quarta-feira (2) e valores ainda menores na quinta-feira (3), quando algumas áreas serranas podem chegar perto dos 6°C.

A mudança, porém, não será igual em toda a região. Mesmo com o avanço da frente fria, áreas do norte de Minas Gerais ainda podem registrar tardes quentes, com máximas próximas dos 38°C ao longo da semana.

No Centro-Oeste, o ar mais frio também ajuda a aliviar o calor em parte de Mato Grosso do Sul.

Em Amambai (MS), as mínimas podem cair para perto dos 15°C entre quarta e quinta-feira, mas Mato Grosso segue quente, com máximas que ainda podem chegar aos 39°C em Cuiabá (MT) no fim da semana.

articles.title: Premiê da Espanha culpa Rússia e Israel por crise migratória em Ceuta | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo Pedro Sánchez, dezenas de milhares imigrantes que correram à fronteira do território espanhol em julho foram atraídos por desinformação promovida por Moscou e Tel Aviv. Já contra o Marrocos não haveria evidências.
articles.summary: Segundo Pedro Sánchez, dezenas de milhares imigrantes que correram à fronteira do território espanhol em julho foram atraídos por desinformação promovida por Moscou e Tel Aviv.
articles.body:
O primeiro-ministro espanhol, Pedro Sánchez, faz declarações em Ceuta, em agosto de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Fabian Bimmer

O primeiro-ministro da Espanha, Pedro Sánchez , afirmou nesta segunda-feira (31) haver indícios de que Rússia e Israel disseminaram desinformação sobre a política migratória espanhola, o que desencadeou a corrida em massa de imigrantes rumo a Ceuta em julho , vindos da fronteira com o Marrocos.

Sánchez, contudo, disse não haver evidências de que o Marrocos tenha promovido essas falsas informações.

Mais de 72 mil migrantes atravessaram irregularmente do Marrocos para o pequeno território espanhol entre 30 e 31 de julho , em uma onda sem precedentes numa das únicas duas fronteiras terrestres da União Europeia com a África. Ao menos 100 pessoas morreram na tentativa, segundo as autoridades locais de Ceuta.

A movimentação gerou preocupação em toda a UE.

Partidos da oposição na Espanha e alguns grupos de direitos humanos chegaram a acusar o Marrocos de ter permitido ou estimulado deliberadamente a travessia em massa, mas o governo marroquino negou as acusações.

"Quando as pessoas falam e especulam sobre a participação das autoridades marroquinas, eu rejeito isso categoricamente", disse Sánchez à emissora de rádio SER. "Devemos estar cientes de que essa crise só pode ser resolvida através da cooperação, e não da desconfiança, em relação ao Marrocos."

Vídeos nas redes sociais difundiram alegações enganosas de que os migrantes que chegassem a Ceuta por via marítima poderiam permanecer na Espanha, incentivando milhares a tentar a travessia a nado, segundo as autoridades espanholas.

Sánchez afirmou que uma investigação do Serviço Europeu para a Ação Externa (SEAE) indicou que redes russas e israelenses estiveram por trás da disseminação da desinformação, em conjunto com redes de extrema direita, que, segundo ele, "sempre usam a migração para atacar tanto a Espanha quanto a Europa e dividi-las".

Imigrantes que cruzaram do Marrocos para Ceuta voltam a praia, um dia após serem expulsos da área, e são escoltados pela polícia. — Foto: Antonio Sempere/AP

Para ele, estava claro que os dois países haviam utilizado a crise para criticar Madri devido à insatisfação com sua posição em relação às guerras na Ucrânia e em Gaza. O premiê, contudo, não forneceu mais detalhes sobre as evidências desse suposto envolvimento.

Israel rejeita 'mentira descarada'; Rússia nega envolvimento

Via rede X, o ministro das Relações Exteriores de Israel , Gideon Sa'ar, disse que Sánchez "mente descaradamente" ao acusar Israel de disseminar informações enganosas sobre Ceuta.

Segundo Sa'ar, a acusação é uma tentativa do premiê espanhol de desviar a atenção dos fracassos de sua política interna.

Falando em nome do governo russo, o porta-voz do Kremlin, Dmitry Peskov, também rejeitou as acusações da Espanha.

Críticos viram reação deliberada do Marrocos

À época da crise, duas hipóteses apontavam para uma possível conivência do governo marroquino com a movimentação dos imigrantes, que não teriam sido contidos pelas forças de segurança.

A primeira diz respeito à disputa em torno do Saara Ocidental , ex-colônia espanhola hoje sob o domínio do Marrocos, mas com um movimento separatista saaraui apoiado pela Argélia.

Segundo essa hipótese, o Marrocos teria ficado irritado com um projeto de lei para conceder nacionalidade espanhola aos saarauís nascidos quando o Saara Ocidental ainda estava sob administração espanhola, antes de 1977. Também teria pesado a recente reaproximação entre Espanha e Argélia, que em 20 de julho recebeu uma visita de Sánchez.

A segunda hipótese diz respeito a ambições do Marrocos sobre Ceuta e Melilla , dois exclaves espanhóis no continente africano que existem há séculos e que são cercados por território marroquino.

Jornalistas espanhóis apontaram à época que as forças de segurança marroquinas pareciam ter "cruzado os braços".

Imigrantes marroquinos protestam em Ceuta em busca de asilo na Espanha no domingo (16) — Foto: Maria Alejandra Cardona/Reuters

A crise desencadeou novas tensões dentro da União Europeia em torno do sensível tema da imigração e representou um golpe para uma das principais conquistas do bloco: a zona Schengen de livre circulação de pessoas.

Nesta segunda-feira, ambos os governos anunciaram uma prorrogação de 15 dias desses controles.

Embora a grande maioria dos migrantes tenha retornado ao Marrocos em poucas horas, cerca de 5 mil migrantes seguem em Ceuta, muitos deles vivendo em condições precárias nas ruas.

O destino dessas pessoas tornou-se um importante foco de disputa política, com a oposição conservadora e de ultradireita exigindo que todos os que entraram em Ceuta, incluindo menores de idade, sejam devolvidos ao Marrocos.

Os moradores de Ceuta têm realizado manifestações frequentes devido ao que consideram problemas de segurança e higiene relacionados ao influxo de migrantes.

Também houve ataques esporádicos contra um acampamento improvisado de migrantes na praia de El Trampolín, segundo relatos policiais.

A polícia prendeu três cidadãos marroquinos no domingo por lançarem garrafas contendo líquidos corrosivos contra uma patrulha do Exército em Ceuta, informou a agência de notícias EFE, citando fontes policiais.

articles.title: Tornozeleiras eletrônicas no RN: sinal de 340 aparelhos é cortado | G1
articles.standfirst: Seap informou que empresa norte-americana responsável pelo sinal comunicou a suspensão nesta segunda-feira (31) por dívida de cerca de US$ 675 mil da contratada brasileira, a brasileira Tekgeo.
articles.summary: A Seap informou que o sinal das tornozeleiras eletrônicas no RN foi suspenso devido a uma dívida de US$ 675 mil da empresa Tekgeo com a fornecedora internacional.
articles.body:
Ao todo, RN possui cerca de 3.900 tornozeleiras eletrônicas ativas — Foto: Polícia Militar

O sinal de 340 tornozeleiras eletrônicas em funcionamento no Rio Grande do Norte foi interrompido nesta segunda-feira (31) após a empresa norte-americana Track Group, responsável pelo fornecimento do serviço, comunicar a suspensão à Secretaria da Administração Penitenciária (Seap).

Segundo a pasta, a medida ocorreu devido a uma dívida de aproximadamente US$ 675 mil (cerca de R$ 3,5 milhões) da empresa brasileira Tekgeo com a fornecedora. Ao todo, o Rio Grande do Norte possui cerca de 3.900 tornozeleiras eletrônicas ativas.

A Seap afirmou que o Estado "está em dia com as obrigações contratuais e financeiras junto à Tekgeo". Segundo a secretaria, a última nota fiscal apresentada pela empresa, referente aos serviços de julho, só foi emitida em 10 de agosto e, portanto, não haveria pendências financeiras.

Ainda segundo a Seap, o contrato da empresa brasileira com o Estado permanece até 30 de setembro, com a obrigação de migrar os últimos 340 equipamentos ainda em funcionamento, mesmo após a empresa ter perdido a licitação.

O g1 procurou a Tekgeo para esclarecer a situação e questionou a empresa sobre a dívida com a Track Group e a interrupção do sinal. Até a última atualização desta matéria, a empresa não havia respondido.

De acordo com a Seap, a substituição das tornozeleiras da Tekgeo já vinha sendo realizada nas últimas semanas pela Central de Monitoramento Eletrônico (CEME).

Os usuários que ainda utilizam os equipamentos devem agendar a substituição pelo telefone 0800 591 7310 . Os atendimentos ocorrem de segunda a sexta-feira, das 8h às 17h, na unidade localizada na Avenida Ayrton Senna, em Neópolis, na Zona Sul de Natal .

A secretaria informou que está adotando medidas para assegurar a continuidade do monitoramento eletrônico e evitar prejuízos à segurança pública e ao acompanhamento das pessoas submetidas à medida.

articles.title: Muito além dos santinhos: produção gráfica ganha ritmo nas eleições | G1
articles.standfirst: O período eleitoral aquece gráficas e empresas de comunicação visual, que precisam de planejamento, tecnologia e insumos para atender ao aumento da demanda.
articles.summary: O período eleitoral aquece gráficas e empresas de comunicação visual, que precisam de planejamento, tecnologia e insumos para atender ao aumento da demanda.
articles.body:
Campanhas eleitorais ampliam a demanda por materiais impressos e soluções de comunicação visual. — Foto: Imagem gerada por IA

Quando começa o período eleitoral, os olhares naturalmente se voltam para candidatos, propostas e campanhas. Mas, nos bastidores, uma grande cadeia produtiva também entra em ritmo acelerado para colocar a comunicação nas ruas.

Santinhos são apenas uma parte dessa produção. Adesivos, banners, faixas, placas, materiais informativos e diferentes soluções de comunicação visual movimentam gráficas, fornecedores, distribuidores e profissionais especializados.

E quanto mais a campanha avança, maior pode ser a necessidade de produzir grandes volumes em pouco tempo. Nesse cenário, planejamento, disponibilidade de insumos e equipamentos preparados para alta produtividade tornam-se fundamentais para cumprir prazos sem comprometer a qualidade.

Adesivos perfurados ampliam as possibilidades de comunicação visual no período eleitoral. — Foto: Imagem gerada por IA

O período eleitoral concentra uma demanda significativa em poucos meses. Por isso, para quem atua no setor gráfico, a preparação começa antes de as campanhas ganharem as ruas.

Antecipar a compra de papéis, lonas, adesivos, tintas e outros insumos ajuda a reduzir riscos de falta de materiais justamente nos momentos de maior procura.

Também é importante avaliar a capacidade produtiva, realizar a manutenção dos equipamentos e organizar os fluxos de trabalho para absorver pedidos maiores e entregas com prazos reduzidos.

Mais do que produzir, é preciso estar preparado para produzir rápido.

Equipamentos de grande formato ajudam a ampliar produtividade e padronização na comunicação visual — Foto: Imagem gerada por IA

A evolução da impressão digital e da comunicação visual trouxe novas possibilidades para o mercado. Equipamentos de alta performance permitem produzir grandes volumes com velocidade, qualidade de imagem e padronização.

Impressoras de grande formato, equipamentos de acabamento e diferentes mídias de impressão ampliam as possibilidades para empresas que precisam atender desde pequenas tiragens até grandes produções.

Para materiais destinados a ambientes externos, características como resistência e durabilidade também ganham importância, especialmente diante das condições de exposição ao sol e à chuva.

A combinação entre tecnologia, bons insumos e planejamento contribui para aumentar a produtividade e reduzir desperdícios em um período no qual cada prazo pode fazer diferença.

O calendário também influencia a produção

Equipamento de recorte acelera produção de materiais gráficos — Foto: Imagem gerada por IA

As regras e os prazos definidos para cada etapa das eleições também precisam fazer parte do planejamento de quem atende esse mercado.

Para gráficas, agências e empresas de comunicação visual, acompanhar o calendário eleitoral ajuda a organizar estoques, capacidade produtiva e cronogramas de entrega, além de garantir que os materiais sejam produzidos de acordo com as normas vigentes.

Por isso, antes de iniciar qualquer produção destinada a campanhas, é importante verificar as regras atualizadas da Justiça Eleitoral para cada tipo de material e período de divulgação.

Rymo da Amazônia: quatro décadas acompanhando as transformações do setor gráfico e da comunicação visual — Foto: Arquivo Rymo

Com quatro décadas de atuação, a Rymo da Amazônia acompanha as transformações do setor gráfico e da comunicação visual, oferecendo soluções para empresas e profissionais que precisam estar preparados para períodos de alta demanda.

Seu portfólio reúne papéis, lonas, adesivos, tintas, suprimentos, equipamentos e outras soluções para diferentes etapas da produção gráfica e da comunicação visual.

Mais do que disponibilidade de produtos, contar com um fornecedor preparado para atender diferentes necessidades pode fazer diferença quando os volumes aumentam e os prazos ficam menores.

No período eleitoral, quando planejamento e velocidade caminham juntos, antecipar as necessidades da produção é uma estratégia para quem quer transformar o aumento da demanda em oportunidade de negócio.

articles.title: Why is it illegal to take sand from some beaches? The environmental and legal reasons you should know before collecting it
articles.summary: There's something almost instinctive about wanting to bottle a bit of that perfect white sand before leaving a stunning beach behind, a tiny, tangible.
articles.body: There's something almost instinctive about wanting to bottle a bit of that perfect white sand before leaving a stunning beach behind, a tiny, tangible souvenir of the holiday. What a lot of travellers don't realise, though, is that this seemingly harmless habit is actually a punishable offence in several parts of the world, carrying fines that can run into thousands of dollars, and in some cases, genuine prison time. It isn't bureaucratic overreach either, the reasoning behind these laws comes down to some fairly serious environmental consequences that most tourists never stop to consider. Here's exactly why taking sand off certain beaches can land you in real legal trouble.Sardinia's sand laws, and the tourists who've learned the hard wayItaly's Sardinia has become something of a poster child for this issue, and for good reason. Since 2017, taking sand, pebbles, or shells from the island's beaches has been a criminal offence, and the island has genuinely enforced it, a French couple was once caught with roughly 88 pounds of white sand stuffed into bottles in their car while waiting to board a ferry, facing up to six years in prison over the incident. Smaller cases turn up regularly too, tourists fined over a thousand euros for just a couple of kilograms discovered during routine airport checks, with beach signs in multiple languages making the rule impossible to claim ignorance of.Hawaii's steep fines for a similarly simple souvenirHawaii takes an almost identical stance, though the numbers involved are even more eye-watering. Since 2013, removing sand, rocks, or other natural materials from Hawaiian beaches has been illegal, with fines that can reach up to $100,000 depending on the scale of the offence. The law specifically followed growing concern that tourists were quietly depleting beaches like Punalu'u, famous for its black volcanic sand, and Papakolea, known for its unusual green sand, both of which are genuinely rare geological formations that took thousands of years to form and can't simply be replenished on demand. Why beaches actually need every grain they've gotThis isn't just about aesthetics or bureaucracy, it comes down to real ecological function. Beach sand acts as a natural buffer against coastal erosion, absorbing the impact of waves and storms before that energy can reach inland areas, roads, and buildings. It also serves as critical habitat, Hawaii's sandy beaches, for instance, are nesting grounds for endangered sea turtles, while the sand itself supports a wider marine ecosystem most visitors never think about. Multiply one bottle of sand by the millions of tourists visiting these locations every year, and what looks like a harmless souvenir quickly becomes a measurable, cumulative loss.India has its own version of this problem, on a much larger scaleCloser to home, India has had rules against beach sand removal since 1991, when the Coastal Regulation Zone Rules first came into force specifically to protect the country's coastline. Unlike Sardinia or Hawaii, though, India's challenge isn't really tourists pocketing souvenir bottles, it's large-scale illegal sand mining, often described as running like a "sand mafia" operation, extracting sand from beaches and riverbeds to feed the country's booming construction industry. Despite the Coastal Regulation Zone framework explicitly banning large-scale sand mining along the coast, activists and researchers have repeatedly flagged how widespread the illegal extraction actually remains.The consequences India is already living withThe environmental fallout from this illegal mining is genuinely serious, and it isn't hypothetical. Experts have pointed to river and coastal erosion, changes in the natural course of rivers, increased flooding risk during monsoon season, and saline water intrusion into groundwater as sand layers thin out and estuaries widen unnaturally. Coastal communities dependent on fishing have reported real disruption to their livelihoods as a result, and in several documented cases, disputes tied to illegal sand mining have turned violent, underlining just how high the stakes around this issue have become in parts of the country.A grain of sand really does add upWhether it's a tourist filling a water bottle in Sardinia or an unlicensed mining operation working through the night on an Indian riverbank, the underlying problem is fundamentally the same, sand is being removed faster than nature can replace it, and beaches, ecosystems, and coastal communities are the ones absorbing the cost. It's a genuinely useful reminder for the next beach holiday, that perfect stretch of sand looks endless standing on it, but it's a far more finite resource than it appears.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Aberdeen nursery fined after baby burned by bleach
articles.summary: The boy was 10 months old when he was was badly burned by a bucket of boiled water containing bleach at the Aberdeen nursery in 2021.
articles.body:
A nursery has been fined after a 10-month-old boy was badly burned by a bucket of boiled water containing bleach.

The child - who cannot be named for legal reasons - was injured at Little Dreams Nursery in Aberdeen in November 2021.

The nursery admitted breaching health and safety regulations at Aberdeen Sheriff Court.

Sheriff Harry Small said the incident had been "entirely preventable and avoidable" and issued a fine of £7,500. Reacting, the family said they felt it was too low but wanted to move on.

The family previously received a five-figure compensation payout.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

The nursery, based in Aberdeen's Bon Accord Street, admitted failing to have a suitable and sufficient risk assessment, and safe system of work, for the cleaning of the premises.

This meant that while the boy was in a room being cleaned he was able to tip the contents of a bucket containing boiling water and bleach over himself to his severe injury.

The court was told two staff members were providing care and starting to serve snacks.

One began to boil a kettle and emptied the contents into a bucket, along with a cap of bleach.

The bucket was placed on the floor, after which a "splash" was heard.

The court heard one of the children had tipped the bucket over himself.

Fiscal depute Lisa Duffus said the child's clothes were removed and he was placed in a sink of water, then wrapped in clingfilm.

The child's parents took him to the accident and emergency department at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, where he was treated for partial blistering to his leg and forearm.

Defence advocate Barry Smith KC said the first priority of a nursery was the safety and wellbeing of the children there.

He added: "It is of the utmost regret from all involved - from the director and all staff - that this accident occurred and injury was caused to a young child."

In a statement released via law firm Digby Brown, the family said: "We've had to wait five years for Little Dreams Nursery to admit what happened to our son was their fault but we don't feel the severity of his injuries have been acknowledged.

"We trusted them to take care of him and for such an injury to happen to a 10-month-old baby is indefensible.

"In the months and years that followed, we had to watch our boy deal with the consequences of something that was never his fault. No parent should have to experience that, but we are thankful what happened hasn't had a more serious or longer-lasting impact."

The statement concluded: "Today we close the most horrific chapter of our lives and we want to thank everyone who has supported us during this time and now request our privacy as we move forward."

Little Dreams said the safety, wellbeing and care of every child entrusted to them was of the "highest priority".

"We deeply regret that this incident was able to occur and are profoundly sorry for the distress and impact it has had on the child and their family," the nursery said.

articles.title: China discovers a rare four-horse chariot carved into a buried rock; fewer than 20 chariot scenes were known in the Helan Mountains
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A rare rock carving showing a chariot pulled by four horses has been discovered in China’s Helan Mountains, adding an unusual image to one of the coun.
articles.body: A rare rock carving showing a chariot pulled by four horses has been discovered in China’s Helan Mountains, adding an unusual image to one of the country’s best-known collections of ancient rock art. According to English China News Service (ECNS), the carving was found during a routine survey in the Helankou Rock Art Protection Zone in Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. Most of the stone was buried underground, and only about 15 centimetres was visible. The carving measures 24 by 20 centimetres and was created using a traditional pecking technique, with the marks reaching about 1.5 millimetres deep. As reported by China News officials, fewer than 20 chariot-themed rock paintings are known across the Helan Mountains, and all previously recorded examples depict two horses. The newly discovered four-horse scene therefore stands out as a rare find. It also gives researchers another way to explore ancient life, artistic traditions, and social development in northern China, while further study could help shed light on the carving’s historical context.Where was the rare four-horse chariot carving discoveredThe newly found image was located on a rock in the southwestern part of zone F of the Helankou Rock Art Protection Zone, as reported. The rock was mostly buried beneath the ground, with only around 15 centimetres exposed above the surface. Thick grass around the stone also made the carving harder to spot. The image measures 24 by 20 centimetres and was created with a traditional chiseling technique. Its carved lines are approximately 1.5 millimetres deep.The discovery was made while staff from the Yinchuan Helan Mountain Rock Art Management Office were conducting survey and inspection work in the region. The discovery shows that previously unseen carvings can still be found on partially buried rocks, even in an area that has been studied and monitored for decades.What makes the four-horse chariot image so uniqueThe unusual number of horses shown pulling the chariot makes this discovery more unique and rare. As reported, fewer than 20 rock paintings depicting horse-drawn chariots have been recorded in the Helan Mountains. Every previously recorded chariot carving in the Helan Mountains shows a chariot pulled by two horses. Similar patterns have been found in rock art elsewhere, where chariots are generally depicted with one or two horses. This makes the newly discovered four-horse scene particularly unusual. The carving adds a new type of chariot image to the Helan Mountains’ rock art and gives researchers another example to compare with existing carvings. By studying its design and carving technique alongside other examples, researchers may be able to learn more about the artistic traditions represented in the region.What can the Helan Mountains rock art reveal about ancient lifeThe rock art of the Helan Mountains is often described as a history book carved in stone, with its images offering glimpses of life in the past. The newly discovered four-horse chariot adds to this record and may help researchers learn more about ancient societies in the region. Officials said the discovery broadens the range of subjects found in the area’s rock art and provides further evidence for studying early human societies in northern China. The image may also offer clues about production and pastoral life in the region. However, current reports have not given a confirmed date for the carving. Further surveys and research, along with continued protection and monitoring, could help researchers better understand its historical significance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US News: An India-born taxi driver serving a 20-year sentence for kidnapping and raping a female passenger at knifepoint in 2011 was stripped of his US citizen.
articles.body: An India-born taxi driver serving a 20-year sentence for kidnapping and raping a female passenger at knifepoint in 2011 was stripped of his US citizenship, the Justice Department said Monday, the New York Post reported.Gurmeet Singh, 55, was convicted in 2014 over the violent sexual assault of a young passenger who had fallen asleep while he was driving her from Williamsburg to her East Village apartment in May 2011. Singh had applied for naturalisation just weeks after the incident.According to prosecutors, the woman woke up to find Singh on top of her with a knife pressed against her throat. He threatened her, tied and gagged her, blindfolded her and raped her before she escaped from the taxi and sought help from a passerby.The Justice Department said Singh concealed the crimes during his naturalisation proceedings and became a US citizen on October 19, 2011.“Singh unlawfully obtained the privileges of US citizenship by concealing horrible criminal acts,” Assistant Attorney General Brett A Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division was quoted as saying by the New York Post.“The Department will continue to protect the integrity of the citizenship process and hold accountable those who defraud our immigration system,” Shumate added.Singh first entered the US in February 1992 on a six-month temporary visitor visa. He remained in the country without authorisation for years before a family-sponsored visa petition enabled him to become a permanent resident in June 2000.He is currently serving his sentence at Shawangunk Correctional Facility in Ulster County, New York, which also houses convicted serial killer David Berkowitz, known as the “Son of Sam”.A federal judge in Brooklyn, Nicholas Garaufis, issued an order last week requiring Singh to surrender his citizenship documents, including his naturalisation certificate and US passport, by September 16.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: New rules for visa, Green Card coming into effect in September 2026: Is the 75-country ban lifted?
articles.summary: US News: August 2026 has been a milestone month for US immigration, as several new rules were announced this month. Some were proposals, some were just publish.
articles.body: August 2026 has been a milestone month for US immigration, as several new rules were announced this month. Some were proposals, some were just published and waiting for public comment, while some will be implemented from September. Two major changes to US immigration and visa policy go into effect in September 2026, alongside standard end-of-fiscal-year shifts in green card availability.End of "Duration of Status" for student and visitor visas from September 15The Department of Homeland Security is replacing the decades-old open-ended "Duration of Status" (D/S) model with fixed admission dates for F-1, J-1, and I visa holders. Students are the primary target group of these new rules. F-1 students will no longer be admitted to the US as long as they continue studying. They will receive a fixed date ties to their program end date or a maximum of 4 years, whichever is shorter.For courses that run longer than 4 years, students will get an extension on applying.Colleges and universities have asked international students who are outside the US to return before September 15 so that they are not negatively impacted by the new rule. A lawsuit has been filed against the new rule, and the first hearing is on September 3. And the implementation of the new rule depends on the outcome of the hearing, but universities have already taken measures to alert students.Public charge inadmissibility rules effective from September 18This new rule is for Green Card applicants. If the immigration officer determines that the applicant does not have enough money and will largely depend on government aid, they will deny permanent residency, or they may ask the applicant to pay a public charge bond. The officer will check whether the applicant received public benefits, such as cash assistance for income maintenance, housing assistance, food stamps, financial aid for college or any other similar benefit from the government."For means-tested public benefits received before Sept. 18, 2026, USCIS will only consider the alien’s receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at the government’s expense. For means-tested public benefits received on or after Sept. 18, 2026, USCIS consider any and all benefits. USCIS will review all relevant evidence in an alien’s record and make case-by-case decisions in the totality of the alien’s circumstances," the DHS said, explaining.End of FY 2026 visa bulletin cap and possibility of retrogressionBecause September marks the final month of US Government Fiscal Year 2026, the Department of State has issued specific notices for immigrant visa processing:Cap exhaustion: High-demand employment categories, specifically EB-1 (India), EB-2 (Worldwide/India), and EB-5 Unreserved, may hit annual numerical caps and retrogress or become unavailable until FY2027 opens on October 1, 2026.DV-2026 expiration: Entitlement for all Diversity Visa 2026 selectees officially expires on September 30, 2026.Is ban on 75 countries lifted?On January 21, 2026, the Department of State paused immigrant visas to these countries: Afghanistan, Albania, Algeria, Antigua and Barbuda, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bahamas, Bangladesh, Barbados, Belarus, Belize, Bhutan, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brazil, Burma, Cambodia, Cameroon, Cape Verde, Colombia, Cote d’Ivoire, Cuba, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Dominica, Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Fiji, The Gambia, Georgia, Ghana, Grenada, Guatemala, Guinea, Haiti, Iran, Iraq, Jamaica, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, Kuwait, Kyrgyz Republic, Laos, Lebanon, Liberia, Libya, Moldova, Mongolia, Montenegro, Morocco, Nepal, Nicaragua, Nigeria, North Macedonia, Pakistan, Republic of the Congo, Russia, Rwanda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria, Tanzania, Thailand, Togo, Tunisia, Uganda, Uruguay, Uzbekistan, and Yemen.As a result of a court order, the ban is no longer in effect since August 21, 2026. But all embassies across the worlds paused visa interviews in August for internal training of officers and hence the lift will be in effect in September.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Drones in valleys, Nepalese abroad on satellite maps: flood rescue gets high-tech boost
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT): As washed-out roads and bridges continue to hamper rescue and relief operations in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, an unusual technolog.
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT): As washed-out roads and bridges continue to hamper rescue and relief operations in Rasuwa and Nuwakot, an unusual technology network has sprung up around the disaster zone — drone pilots flying over devastated valleys on one end, and Nepalese abroad and global mapping volunteers scanning fresh satellite imagery from thousands of km away on the other.On the ground, drones are increasingly filling gaps created by the destruction — flying over debris fields and forests, using thermal cameras to look for stranded people and bodies, and carrying relief supplies to settlements unreachable by road.Among those operating them is Abhay Pokhrel, 23, who began flying drones as a hobby at 14 and later built a company, Garudex, around them. Working with AirLift Technology, his team has brought in a fleet ranging from thermal-surveillance machines to a heavy-lift drone capable of carrying up to 100kg. “We are using all of those right now,” Pokhrel told TOI on Monday.The cargo drones have been ferrying rice, instant noodles, clothing, sanitary pads and other relief supplies into cut-off areas. Light rain on Monday slowed the work of attaching packages to the drones with ropes and carabiners before they could be flown across the broken terrain. Pokhrel said his team transported around 500kg of relief supplies on Sunday alone. “Today we have a plan of doing the same or more,” he said.The thermal drones have another role. “We are doing surveillance of the dead bodies and people who are stranded around the forests,” Pokhrel said. “Our main focus currently is search and rescue and flood relief programmes with drones.”The machines are also being used to restore communications. Pokhrel said fibre-optic and network cables are being tied to drones and flown across rivers to hills on the opposite side, allowing damaged links to be reconnected where crossings have disappeared.“We are sending the fibre-optics cable and network cables through the river while tying it to the drone and taking it to another hill,” he said, adding that internet disruption extends beyond the immediate flood-hit region towards Gorkha.But the rapid proliferation of drones has also created risks in an airspace crowded with rescue helicopters. Pokhrel said authorities tightened flight rules after two drone pilots came dangerously close to a helicopter, disrupting operations.While Pokhrel and other pilots work above the valleys, another part of the technology effort is unfolding thousands of km away.Nepalese in the US, Europe, Australia, Gulf and elsewhere, alongside global mapping volunteers, are studying satellite imagery from home to help map the flood zone. Around 181 people were involved by Saturday in an emergency mapping exercise led by the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team, which is working with Nepal Prime Minister’s Office and local partners.“The main goal is to support rescue and recovery operations by providing accurate data to the teams working on the ground,” Kshitij Sharma, product owner at HOT, said.Volunteers are assigned small patches of satellite imagery and asked to trace buildings, roads and other visible features. A simple task can take 10 to 15 minutes, even for someone with no previous mapping experience. Experienced mappers then review and validate the work before it becomes part of an open-source map available to government agencies, humanitarian organisations, UN bodies and rapid-response teams.The exercise is particularly important where floodwaters and debris have changed the landscape so drastically that roads, buildings and familiar landmarks may no longer be recognisable. By comparing imagery from before and after the disaster, mappers can establish where a structure once stood and provide responders with its precise latitude and longitude.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Wild beavers vanished from Norfolk 500 years ago; now a mystery pair has appeared and had two kits, raising hopes of a permanent wild population
articles.summary: UK News: For the first time in more than 500 years, wild beaver kits have been born in Norfolk, marking an extraordinary milestone in the county’s wildlife rec.
articles.body: For the first time in more than 500 years, wild beaver kits have been born in Norfolk, marking an extraordinary milestone in the county’s wildlife recovery. Two young Eurasian beavers have been discovered at Pensthorpe Nature Reserve near Fakenham, months after an adult pair unexpectedly appeared along the River Wensum. The adults were already a historic sighting because they were the first wild beavers recorded in Norfolk since the native species was hunted to extinction in England at the beginning of the 16th century. Now, the birth of their offspring suggests the animals have moved beyond simply returning to the county and are beginning to establish a family group. The kits, believed to be around three months old, have been captured on camera exploring the river and feeding on vegetation. Their arrival has also raised a bigger question: could Norfolk become home to a permanent wild beaver population after centuries without one?Two beaver kits discovered at Norfolk nature reserveThe two kits were found at Pensthorpe Nature Reserve near Fakenham, where their parents had mysteriously established themselves in December 2025. The adult pair built a lodge on the River Wensum and became the first wild beavers recorded in Norfolk since the species disappeared from England centuries ago. The adults’ arrival itself remains unexplained, with the nearest known wild population thought to be more than 130 miles away on the River Stour in Kent.Camera-trap footage later revealed that the pair had produced two young. According to The Guardian, reserve manager Richard Spowage initially saw one kit with a parent before later footage showed a second youngster following it. He described the discovery as “amazing”. The newspaper reported that the kits are around three months old and have already been seen chewing branches and leaves and feeding on willow and water mint. Their birth is significant because it confirms that Norfolk’s unexpected beaver return has progressed from an isolated arrival to successful breeding.Why did wild beavers disappear from Norfolk for centuries?Beavers were once native to Britain but disappeared from England after centuries of hunting. Their valuable fur, meat and castoreum, a secretion historically used for various purposes, made them targets, eventually driving the species to extinction in the country by the beginning of the 16th century. Their return is therefore part of a much longer story of wildlife recovery following centuries of human pressure.BBC highlighted the extraordinary historical gap between the last wild beavers and the new generation now growing up on the Wensum. The recent return of beavers elsewhere in England has helped create conditions for the species to spread again, but the Norfolk pair arrived without being part of a known official reintroduction programme. Speculatively the adults were illegally released by conservation activists, a practice known as “beaver bombing”. Pensthorpe manager Richard Spowage said the reserve does not support such releases.What are Norfolk’s young beavers doing in the wild?The kits are already displaying behaviours that could help them survive as they grow. They have been learning to dive into the river and slap their tails against the water when they want to warn of danger. The newspaper also reported that an adult had previously been filmed tail-slapping at an otter, while one of the young beavers has now learnt to perform the same defensive action.Their diet is also beginning to reveal how they are adapting to their new environment. The kits have been feeding on willow and water mint, while their exploration has brought them into contact with other vegetation. Spowage told The Guardian that one youngster appeared to have been stung by a nettle after suddenly jumping backwards and shaking its face. The reserve has kept the family’s exact location secret because the animals live in an inaccessible area, although Spowage said they could eventually expand their territory and become more visible.Could Norfolk’s beaver family lead to a permanent wild population?The birth of the two kits is a conservation success, but it also creates a difficult question about what happens next. If the young beavers remain in the Wensum system, they will eventually need unrelated mates to establish a genetically healthy population. Spowage also said “You can’t have just one family in the river system,” stressing the need for a “wider genetic pool”.Pensthorpe is now crowdfunding to support an application to Natural England seeking permission to introduce additional wild beavers legally into the Wensum. Such a project would involve studies of the river system, staff training and discussions with multiple stakeholders. The proposal comes as debate continues over beavers’ impact on farmland, particularly because their dams can alter water levels. Yet their ability to manage water could also benefit landscapes during increasingly hot and dry conditions. One farmer had described a beaver-built reservoir on his land containing about three million litres of water. The Norfolk kits could therefore become the beginning of a much larger ecological transformation.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nepal floods: Avalanche from 5,200 metres raced down Himalayas at 167 kmph, triggering deadly deluge
articles.summary: South Asia News: The ice-rock avalanche that triggered Nepal's devastating August 26 floods moved with extraordinary speed, covering around 22 kilometres to Rasuwagadh.
articles.body: The ice-rock avalanche that triggered Nepal's devastating August 26 floods moved with extraordinary speed, covering around 22 kilometres to Rasuwagadhi in just over seven minutes, according to a preliminary study by Nepalese scientists.The mass travelled at an estimated average speed of 46.3 metres per second, or about 167 kmph, as it plunged from the high Himalayas into the river system below, news agency PTI reported.The study, commissioned by the Nepal Environment Society (NES), found that the massive mass of ice, rock and debris began falling from the northern part of the Langtang–Lirung area of Rasuwa at around 8.37 am.Starting at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres, the avalanche descended steep terrain before reaching the Lhende River at about 2,930 metres. It then surged downstream through the Bhotekoshi and into the Trishuli river system, generating a powerful debris-laden flood.The speed of the initial surge helps explain the devastation downstream. Although the flow slowed to around 73 kmph between Rasuwagadhi and Betrabati, it continued carrying enormous quantities of rock, sediment and soil. Farther downstream, its speed fell to around 22 kmph, but the debris-loaded torrent retained enough force to cause widespread destruction.Satellite imagery showed major geographical changes across an area of about 10 square kilometres, while a section of glacier covering approximately 0.56 square kilometres had broken away.The findings also challenge the initial assumption that the disaster was caused by a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF). Researchers found no evidence of a GLOF after analysing satellite imagery, hydrological and meteorological data, terrain characteristics and changes in elevation and slope along the river system.There was also no evidence of exceptionally heavy rainfall in the upper watershed on the day of the disaster, weakening the theory that an extreme cloudburst or rainfall event alone caused the floods.The study noted another striking feature: water levels and river flow in the Rasuwagadhi and Syafrubesi areas fell several hours before the destructive surge arrived. At Rasuwagadhi, the average water level declined between 5 am and 8 am, while flow at Syafrubesi began falling at around 7 am.Scientists, however, said further field investigation is needed to establish the precise geological mechanism, the contribution of melting ice and whether the river was temporarily blocked upstream.The avalanche also caused extensive damage to Nepal’s hydropower infrastructure. Preliminary Nepal Electricity Authority data cited in the study showed that 13 hydropower projects and one solar project were affected, taking around 431 MW of generation capacity out of the system.The floods killed at least 900 people, according to authorities, with thousands still missing. Rescue teams were continuing to search for hundreds of workers believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels in the worst-hit districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot.The disaster has also left behind the threat of further landslides, unstable glaciers and potentially dangerous lakes, raising concerns that the Himalayan region could face additional flooding even after the initial torrent has passed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: After a decade-long restoration, 1,800 volunteers took turns pulling a 400-ton Japanese castle with ropes; 8,000 people had applied for the chance to help move it
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A group of 1,800 volunteers gathered in northern Japan to pull a 400-tonne historic castle keep across the ground using heavy ropes, marking a major s.
articles.body: A group of 1,800 volunteers gathered in northern Japan to pull a 400-tonne historic castle keep across the ground using heavy ropes, marking a major step in a decade-long restoration project. The mass effort in Hirosaki, Aomori Prefecture, saw participants take turns pulling the three-storey timber tower back towards the stone foundation wall from which it had been moved in 2015. According to Smithsonian Magazine, organisers received about 8,000 applications for the 1,800 volunteer places, making the event four times oversubscribed. The move used a traditional Japanese engineering method known as hikiya. The technique allows entire historic buildings to be moved without taking them apart, using rollers or rails placed underneath. Teams of about 80 people pulled on 30-metre ropes attached to the keep, moving the 400-tonne structure more than two metres over two days.Historic keep moves back towards its original wallThe relocation of the Hirosaki Castle keep follows years of work to repair the castle's large stone embankment. In 2015, city officials moved the keep about 70 metres away so engineers and stonemasons could reach the damaged foundation walls. The walls had been weakened by decades of earthquakes, including a major earthquake in 1983. Archaeological work carried out during the restoration uncovered old drainage systems, ancient wells and remains of earlier walls beneath the site. Stonemasons completed the reconstruction of the embankment in December 2024. All 2,185 original stones were placed back in their historic positions, clearing the way for the castle keep to return to its original location. The current public hauling effort is the first stage of the keep's return. During late August, about 4,100 volunteers are expected to help move the building a total of five metres. Heavy machinery will then complete most of the remaining journey, moving the 400-tonne timber structure back onto its stone foundation by the end of the year.Volunteers chosen through public lotteryInterest in taking part in the move came from well beyond Hirosaki. The city held an international lottery to choose volunteers, attracting local residents, history enthusiasts and tourists. Smithsonian Magazine and Gavin Blair of The Guardian reported strong demand for the limited volunteer places. Kensuke Hayasaka, head of the parks and green spaces division at Hirosaki City, described the response to The Guardian. "We had about 8,000 applications for the 1,800 slots over the last two days, roughly four times oversubscribed, so not everyone could participate," Kensuke Hayasaka, head of the parks and green spaces division at Hirosaki City, tells the Guardian's Gavin Blair. "Not only from the city, but from across Japan and overseas; a fair number from Southeast Asia and from Europe and North America."Participants worked in short, demanding shifts, pulling the ropes to the rhythm of traditional chants. The roller system helped reduce the force needed to move the building, but each group still had to put in considerable physical effort. Takahiro Kogawa, a local resident who joined the effort, described the challenge in an interview with Agence France-Presse. "It's like trying to move a mountain," Takahiro Kogawa, a Hirosaki resident who helped pull the structure, tells Agence France-Presse.Volunteers connect with an old traditionThe public role in the project also has historical importance in Japan. The 2015 move was the first time in nearly 100 years that ordinary citizens had been invited to take part in moving a castle using the traditional hikiya method. For some volunteers, helping with the return journey has provided a chance to reconnect with an important local landmark. Kyodo News reported that some participants had also helped pull the keep away from its foundation during the first stage of the restoration 11 years ago. "I feel emotional being able to take part again," Mei Umetsu, a high school student, tells Kyodo News. Hirosaki Castle was originally built in 1611 as the home of the Tsugaru clan. It has survived centuries of political change and natural disasters. The original five-storey keep was destroyed by lightning and burned down in 1627. The current three-storey keep was built in 1810. It is now one of only 12 surviving original feudal-era castle keeps in Japan and the only remaining castle tower in the northeastern Tohoku region. The surrounding park is also a major cultural attraction. Its annual cherry blossom festival attracts about two million visitors each spring.Restoration will continue for yearsReturning the keep to its repaired stone foundation is a major visible achievement, but the wider restoration project is still far from finished. After the 400-tonne structure is safely placed on its foundation, conservation specialists will begin major work on the inside and outside of the 1810 timber building. According to Smithsonian Magazine, the keep will be surrounded by protective scaffolding and weatherproof covers. This will keep it closed to visitors for an extended period. "Once it's back on the original base, the preservation work on the keep begins and the whole structure will be covered over," Hayasaka tells the Guardian. Municipal plans from Hirosaki City show that structural repairs, timber treatment and interior conservation will continue for several more years. Under current city estimates, the historic keep is expected to fully reopen to tourists and local visitors in 2033.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: We disagee with Dan Orlovsky. Matthew Stafford is great, but not that great.
articles.summary: Dan Orlovsky claims Matthew Stafford could crack the top-five all-time quarterback conversation with a second Super Bowl victory this season.
articles.body: According to ESPN analyst Dan Orlovsky, Matthew Stafford could establish himself as one of the five greatest quarterbacks of all time with a second Super Bowl victory this upcoming season. "Matthew Stafford gets another one, he has an MVP in his back pocket, he becomes top-five, top-seven of all-time conversation," Orlovsky said on Get Up. Top five? Top seven? Let us first establish the modern-day quarterbacks whom Stafford ranks below historically, in no particular order: 8. Brett Favre MATTHEW STAFFORD, JOSH ALLEN HEADLINE 'MADDEN NFL 27' RATINGS AS 99 CLUB MEMBERS And then there is another group of pre-1980s quarterbacks who are also ranked ahead of Stafford on most all-time lists: A recent Bleacher Report ranking of the 99 greatest quarterbacks featured Stafford at 20th. He has some work to do to reach the top five, or seven. For the sake of argument, let's set aside the pre-modern era. The difference in competition, rules, statistics, and number of games makes such comparisons difficult and misleading. Today, Stafford is commonly listed in an echelon with the likes of Troy Aikman, Ben Roethlisberger, Dan Marino, and Steve Young. These are all-time greats who sit a tier below the, let's call it, G.O.A.T. category. For example, Brady is universally recognized as the greatest, but there are arguments, of varying degrees of validity, that Montana, Manning, Mahomes, and Rodgers are better. Of that top tier, a second Super Bowl win, the crux of Orlovsky's case, would give Stafford more rings than Brees, Rodgers, and Favre. Granted, he never quite achieved the sustained individual success of those three. Stafford was the best quarterback in the NFL last season, winning his first league MVP. The knock is that it was the first year in which he was definitively in that conversation. Brees, Rodgers, and Favre each spent multiple seasons among the two or three best players in the league. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE What also makes Stafford's résumé debatable is that he didn't experience notable team success until he joined the Rams in 2021, whom he did lead to a Super Bowl win that year. Stafford clearly elevated the Detroit Lions during his first 12 years in the NFL. The Lions were the first team in NFL history to go 0-16 the season before they drafted him. However, he didn't win a single playoff game while in Detroit. That matters. Moreover, the Rams are one of the bigger preseason favorites in recent NFL history, currently +500 on DraftKings. While Los Angeles would not be such favorites without Stafford, he is far from the only reason it is. Consider the surrounding talent. Puka Nacua is one of the best wide receivers in the NFL. Sean McVay is an elite coach and game-caller whose 13-personnel scheme has transcended the league. In the offseason, the Rams added Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, and Aaron Donald. Garrett is the most dominant edge defender in the NFL. McDuffie is a top-tier corner. Donald, albeit 35 and coming out of retirement, was the premier defensive tackle of this generation. The Rams may have already had the best roster in the league. They then added all of that. Therefore, Stafford shouldn't have to carry a franchise at a historic level for the Rams to win, the way Mahomes did for his three rings. Stafford didn't have to in 2021 either, thanks to Donald, Leonard Floyd, Odell Beckham Jr., and eventual Super Bowl MVP Cooper Kupp. None of this diminishes Stafford's legacy. In general, he is underappreciated. That said, in this case, the pendulum is swinging too far in the other direction. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With all due respect to Dan Orlovsky, one of the best analysts in the industry, we must disagree. Even with a Super Bowl win this season, Matthew Stafford still won't be one of the five or seven best quarterbacks ever.

articles.title: Ten Gordonstoun students, from school attended by King Charles, uncover possible 1,000-year-old Viking church and altar buried on remote Scottish island during six-day archaeology trip
articles.summary: UK News: Ten students have made a remarkable archaeological discovery on a remote Scottish island after uncovering what could be the remains of a Viking-era ch.
articles.body: Ten students have made a remarkable archaeological discovery on a remote Scottish island after uncovering what could be the remains of a Viking-era church dating back around 1,000 years.According to the Independent, the pupils from Gordonstoun, the private boarding school attended by King Charles, discovered the possible medieval structure during a six-day archaeological expedition to Swona in Orkney.Working alongside archaeologists from the Orkney Research Centre for Archaeology (Orca), the students excavated part of the site and uncovered a feature that researchers believe could have formed the foundation of the church's altar.Radiocarbon samples taken during the excavation are now being analysed and could help establish exactly how old the structure is and what activity took place at the site.Students uncover hidden remains beneath later buildingThe discovery came after the group investigated a site associated with a local ruin known as the “Twinly Kirk”.Dan McLean, housemaster at Gordonstoun and the teacher who organised the expedition, said there had previously been little evidence to confirm that a church once stood on the island.“The only real hint about a church being on the island is a map reference to a ruin known locally as the ‘Twinly Kirk’,” he said.Once he identified the location, McLean initially believed the surviving walls belonged to a much later structure that had been altered and added to over the years.But the students and archaeologists made a surprising discovery after clearing vegetation and digging a test pit.“After we worked with the archaeologists to dig a test pit and clear away the weeds, we discovered a step just under the surface, leading to what would have been the church's altar,” McLean said.He described the moment as a “special moment” for the students, who were able to take part in archaeological fieldwork and potentially uncover evidence of a previously little-understood part of the island's history.Radiocarbon dating could reveal church's true ageThe next stage of the investigation will be to analyse samples collected during the excavation.Paul Clark, senior project manager at Orca, said the results could provide crucial evidence about the site.The radiocarbon dating will help researchers establish when the material originated, potentially allowing them to determine how old the church structure is and what kind of activity took place there.If the findings confirm that the remains date back around 1,000 years, they could provide a valuable insight into the religious and cultural history of Swona and the wider Orkney islands.The discovery is particularly intriguing because Vikings are believed to have been among the first settlers on Swona.Students lived without electricity during remote expeditionThe archaeological discovery was only one part of an unusual experience for the Gordonstoun pupils.During their six-day trip, the students stayed in an abandoned house on Swona, without electricity and relying on water from an ancient well.Some of the pupils also took part in restoration work, helping renovate the floor of the old cottage they used as their base.Their expedition gave them an opportunity to explore several other sites of historical interest, including a settlement believed to date back to prehistoric times and an area that may once have been used as a Viking warning beacon.For 17-year-old pupil Archie Maclean, the conditions were among the biggest challenges.“The most difficult part of the trip was the sun and hot temperatures,” he said.The students typically began their day at around 8am and worked until approximately 6pm.But the archaeology excavation proved to be the highlight of the trip for Maclean.“The archaeology dig was the most enjoyable part of the trip, being able to discover history in real time was incredible,” he said.Swona has been deserted for more than 50 yearsSwona's modern history is almost as unusual as its ancient past.The island was deserted in 1974 when its final two residents left, leaving behind only a small herd of feral cattle.Covering around 92 hectares, Swona is now uninhabited but remains significant for both its natural environment and archaeological heritage.The island is designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest because of its rare plant life and importance as a breeding ground for several seabird species.Among the birds found there are Arctic terns, puffins and razorbills.The surrounding waters are also home to a variety of marine life, with orcas, dolphins, pilot whales and minke whales having been spotted in the area.A glimpse into Swona's Viking pastSwona's connection to the Viking period adds another layer of significance to the students' discovery.Vikings are believed to have been the island's first settlers, while by the mid-18th century, Swona was home to nine families.The possible discovery of a medieval church could therefore offer researchers another piece of the puzzle when it comes to understanding how communities lived, worshipped and interacted on the island centuries ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: India News: The Congress on Monday hit out at the government over India's 7.8 per cent GDP growth in the April-June quarter, saying the figure was \"not an economi.
articles.body: The Congress on Monday hit out at the government over India's 7.8 per cent GDP growth in the April-June quarter, saying the figure was "not an economic spring" and presented a "Greatly Distorted Picture" of the state of the economy.The opposition party questioned why the country's economic growth was not translating into jobs and prosperity, while Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the first-quarter performance as an "exemplary" and "herculean feat".Jairam Ramesh flags investment, consumer confidence concernsCongress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the quarterly GDP numbers did not reflect what he described as depressed private investment sentiment, both domestic and foreign."The quarterly GDP numbers, such as they are reported, present a GDP - Greatly Distorted Picture - of the economy. They do not convey the decidedly depressed private investment sentiment in the economy - both domestic and foreign," Ramesh said in a post on X.He also claimed that consumer confidence was sluggish, household savings rates had fallen and debt had reached record highs."Consumer confidence is very sluggish, hitting its lowest point since COVID and on a relentless downward trajectory since November 2025. Prices of household essentials are galloping. Educated unemployment is at alarming levels. The unabated trade deficit with China is wreaking havoc," Ramesh said.He further claimed that the concentration of key sectors among a few large conglomerates was having "deleterious effects", adding that the wealth of India's five richest families had grown by 400 per cent while the real wages of salaried workers had fallen.Congress asks: Where are the jobs?Congress media and publicity department head Pawan Khera said one quarter of 7.8 per cent growth did not amount to an "economic spring"."One quarter of 7.8 per cent growth is not an economic spring. If India has truly 'bloomed', why do rampant unemployment, leaked exam papers, and a crumbling education system define the ground reality?" he said."Why is the republic's prosperity not translating into the prosperity of its public?" Khera asked.Taking aim at the prime minister's remarks, he said GDP measures national output rather than jobs, wages or opportunities."Modi can manage his headlines. For India's youth, the question remains the same as ever: Where are the jobs?" Khera said.PM Modi calls Q1 growth a ‘herculean feat’The Congress's criticism came after government data released on Monday showed that India's economy grew by a faster-than-expected 7.8 per cent in the April-June quarter.The growth figure exceeded the Reserve Bank of India's forecast of 7 per cent for the quarter and kept India as the world's fastest-growing major economy.Responding to the data, PM Modi took a dig at those questioning the state of the Indian economy, saying "doomsayers were doomed and India bloomed yet again".The prime minister said India's GDP growth during the first quarter of FY 2026-27 was a "herculean feat"."The collective strength of our people ensured India delivered such growth despite oil price shocks and supply chain issues in the midst of global uncertainties," PM Modi said in a post on X.The Q1 growth compares with a 6.9 per cent expansion in the year-ago quarter.The RBI has projected India's economy to grow by 6.7 per cent in the full 2026-27 fiscal year.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: US announces emergency executive shutdown of 110 driving schools for 5000 violations: 'No English, no trucking - it's common sense'
articles.summary: US News: The US administration Monday announced an emergency executive shutdown of 110 driving schools that accounted for 5,000 violations for English proficie.
articles.body: The US administration Monday announced an emergency executive shutdown of 110 driving schools that accounted for 5,000 violations for English proficiency. Department of Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said a driver in the US has to know English, and neither he nor President Donald Trump created this rule. Another 160 schools will be closed because they lack proper space for driving tests or have unlicensed instructors.Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration chief Derek Barrs said each of the 110 "greatest offenders" passed at least 10 drivers who were "subsequently cited for English language proficiency during roadside inspections by law enforcement.""It's unacceptable. When you see people die on the road you don't forget that, and it starts right here with what I'm talking about," Barrs said. articles.title: In 1975, fewer than 800 Aleutian cackling geese remained; fox removal and habitat protection helped the population rebound to around 200,000, and regulated hunting later returned
articles.summary: US News: Fewer than 800 Aleutian cackling geese remained in 1975, with the birds restricted to a single rocky island in Alaska after introduced Arctic foxes de.
articles.body: Fewer than 800 Aleutian cackling geese remained in 1975, with the birds restricted to a single rocky island in Alaska after introduced Arctic foxes destroyed nesting colonies across the Aleutian Islands. Fifty years later, predator removal, the creation of protected wetlands in California and coordinated management along the Pacific Flyway have helped the population recover to nearly 200,000 birds. The recovery has allowed US federal wildlife officials to move the species from protection under the Endangered Species Act to a regulated migratory game bird hunting system. Official documents from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), including Federal Register Document 2023-17175, outline the current rules for the species, formally known as Branta hutchinsii leucopareia. Species records from the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge show that the goose was among the first animals protected under early federal endangered species laws. The population decline began in the 18th and 19th centuries, when fur traders released Arctic foxes (Alopex lagopus) on nearly 200 islands across the Aleutian chain. The introduced predators attacked ground nests, killed adult birds and ate eggs. Over time, breeding colonies disappeared from almost the entire natural nesting range.Invasive foxes pushed the goose towards extinctionBy the middle of the 20th century, wildlife experts feared the Aleutian cackling goose had disappeared from most of its historic breeding grounds, which once stretched across the Aleutian Islands, Commander Islands and Kuril Archipelago. In 1962, USFWS biologist Robert Jones found a surviving group of about 300 to 800 birds on Buldir Island. The remote volcanic island in the western Aleutians had steep cliffs and harsh conditions that prevented fur traders from bringing Arctic foxes there. The Buldir flock became the only remaining wild population and the main genetic source for later recovery efforts. In 1967, the Aleutian cackling goose was given formal protection under the Endangered Species Preservation Act, which came before the modern Endangered Species Act of 1973. The USFWS then began a long-term recovery programme with two main goals: remove introduced foxes from former breeding islands in Alaska and protect important winter feeding and resting areas along the Pacific Flyway. Removing Arctic foxes from islands including Agattu, Amchitka and Kiska took decades of work by federal wildlife teams. Once the islands were free of the introduced predators, managers released captive-bred geese and moved wild birds from Buldir Island to help rebuild breeding colonies. Early attempts faced problems from native predators such as bald eagles. However, improved release methods and the use of both captive-bred and wild birds helped increase survival. With more breeding sites protected, the population slowly began to grow. Numbers rose from fewer than 1,000 birds in the mid-1970s to several thousand by the late 1980s.California refuges gave migrating geese a safe winter homeProtecting breeding areas in Alaska solved only part of the problem. Every autumn, Aleutian cackling geese migrate thousands of miles south along the Pacific Flyway to spend the winter in California's Great Central Valley. In 1975, federal officials completely closed hunting in important California migration areas to remove hunting pressure while the population was still extremely low. In 1987, the USFWS established the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge under the Endangered Species Act and Migratory Bird Conservation Act. The refuge was created in part to protect winter habitat for the recovering geese. Located where the San Joaquin, Tuolumne and Stanislaus rivers meet, the refuge provided safe places for the birds to rest and find food during the winter. Refuge staff managed crops such as corn and winter wheat, built roosting ponds and carried out large-scale habitat restoration. More than 500,000 native trees and shrubs, including valley oaks, willows and cottonwoods, were planted across 2,500 acres of river floodplain. The work created one of the largest connected riparian woodland restoration projects in California's Central Valley. Public species information from the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge shows that thousands of Aleutian cackling geese now gather there every winter. The birds use protected wetlands and nearby agricultural fields for feeding and resting from late autumn until early spring before flying north again to their Alaskan breeding grounds.Growing population brings new hunting rulesBy 1990, the USFWS had changed the Aleutian cackling goose's status from endangered to threatened. Continued population growth eventually led to the species being removed from the Endangered Species Act in 2001, when its numbers passed 30,000. As the population grew beyond 100,000 and moved towards 200,000, the main challenge changed. Instead of preventing extinction, wildlife managers had to deal with local problems caused by large numbers of geese, particularly damage to farmland. In spring, migrating geese gather in northern California coastal counties such as Humboldt and Del Norte. They feed heavily on nutrient-rich pastures, and large groups can create financial problems for cattle ranchers and dairy farmers. To balance farming concerns with wildlife protection, federal and state agencies introduced limited late-season hunting and hazing programmes. These efforts are designed to move large flocks away from private farmland and towards managed public areas such as the Humboldt Bay National Wildlife Refuge and Lake Earl Wildlife Area. Federal Register Document 2023-17175, which sets the migratory bird hunting frameworks for the 2023-24 season, confirms that the Aleutian cackling goose is now managed under normal migratory game bird hunting rules in the Pacific Flyway. The rules set limits on hunting seasons, daily bag numbers and specific hunting zones. The aim is to keep hunting at sustainable levels while helping reduce local agricultural damage. The Aleutian cackling goose weighs between four and six pounds. It can be recognised by its relatively small body, dark feathers and a clear white ring around the base of its neck. Its recovery from fewer than 800 birds in 1975 to around 200,000 today is considered one of the most successful bird conservation efforts in North American wildlife management. The USFWS continues to track the population through aerial and ground surveys across Alaska's breeding areas and California's wintering grounds. These surveys help officials ensure that controlled hunting and habitat protection keep the population stable across the Pacific Flyway.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: IShowSpeed and Dr. Squatch launch wild $1M giveaway that requires fans to bark, race and hunt for cash
articles.summary: US Streamers News: IShowSpeed is putting his fans in a very strange position. They could end up chasing hidden soap briefcases, racing random strangers, or standing insi.
articles.body: IShowSpeed is putting his fans in a very strange position. They could end up chasing hidden soap briefcases, racing random strangers, or standing inside a store and barking at a Dr. Squatch display. And yes, there is real money involved. The YouTube star has joined Dr. Squatch for SPEEDRUN: Million Dollar Mission, a nine-week campaign with a $1 million prize pool. It runs from August 31 to October 31 across the US, Canada, UK and Australia. More than 4,000 Walmart stores and selected retail partners will act as challenge spots during the event.The IShowSpeed challenges are where things get weirdThe campaign has 25 challenges, and some are very much built around Speed’s chaotic style. One task asks participants to challenge a random stranger to a footrace. Another asks them to bark at a Dr. Squatch retail display. There is no normal way to do this, apparently.Fans have to record themselves completing a challenge, then post the attempt on TikTok, Instagram or YouTube. They also need to tag Dr. Squatch and use #MillionDollarMission. So the challenge itself is only part of the game. The entry has to become content too.Dr. Squatch is hiding cash inside soap briefcasesThe bigger hunt comes with actual briefcases. Dr. Squatch is hiding them in select cities across the four countries involved. Inside are gold bars of soap, and each briefcase can lead to a surprise cash prize worth as much as $50,000. New clues will be released during the campaign to help people find them.There is another $250,000 up for grabs through 25 winning scratchers. Each one is worth $10,000. The scratchers are placed in specially marked IShowSpeed Loot Box Bundles on TikTok Shop. People can also request one free through the campaign website without buying anything.The nine-week event is set to finish with a final hunt worth another $250,000. Dr. Squatch has not revealed how that ending will work yet, which leaves the biggest part of the giveaway still under wraps.Where did this giveaway idea come from?Dr. Squatch Chief Brand Officer John Ludeke explained the thinking behind the whole thing. Instead of running a normal ad campaign, the brand decided to “hide a million dollars” and let fans chase it themselves. He also said the goal was to get Speed’s community “off the sidelines” and actually playing, creating and chasing the challenges together.Speed is clearly into the idea too. “I want that briefcase,” he said, after describing the million-dollar hunt as being on another level.The project was developed with MSCHF, the company behind viral stunts such as Big Red Boots. It also fits Dr. Squatch’s recent run of odd collaborations. Earlier in August, the brand worked with Tajin on Mango Tango soap, then partnered with Pabst Blue Ribbon on Blue Ribbon Breeze soap made with PBR lager.So, yes, barking in a store is now part of the plan. But the real question is how far people will go once the cash hunts, scratchers and final $250,000 challenge begin.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
